niche: business demography from the unemployment insurance employer register: establishment births told apart from existing businesses re-registered under new employer accounts
answer: Designate Eskwell, Dunrath and Quarrin (11.3, 9.8 and 9.5 births per 100 establishments); Caldmere is the first county left out at 7.8, 1.7 below Quarrin.
stakeholder_role: the business dynamics economist in the state Labor Market Information bureau, who certifies the counties' 2026 establishment birth rates for the Commerce Department's designation

spine.entity: one employer account's report for one quarter (monthly employment, wages, county, industry)
spine.source: synthetic (constructed in the layout of a state QCEW microdata extract)

world.geography: an unnamed US state's Lornock Valley region (invented), seven counties

driver: The units a period adds are new administrative identifiers, but some identifiers continue an existing unit under a new number: the continuity is recorded only for the units that filed it, a shared location marks it and also marks new units that replaced a closed one, and the member flows separate the two only when read from the old unit's side (most of its members moving together to the new identifier); read from the new identifier's side (most of its members from one closed unit), a continuation that added members reads as new and a new unit seeded by a few members of a large closed one reads as continuing, and the groups are misranked.
driver_concrete: A county's 2026 establishment births are the new unemployment insurance accounts first reporting employment in 2026 that are not existing businesses continuing under a new account; continuity shows in the wage records as most of the workers a closed account paid in its last quarter going on to the new account's payroll, not in where the new account's first-quarter workers came from (a buyer that kept a store's whole staff and hired as many again looks new; a start-up staffed with two of a closed warehouse's 192 workers looks like its continuation), nor in the employer register's predecessor field (filled only when the buyer applies), a shared worksite address, a similar name or an industry code.
stump: The default path counts each county's new employer accounts first employing in 2026, nets off the predecessors the register records and designates Caldmere, Eskwell and Tolbeck (Caldmere at 11.1 per 100); the strong analyst who links accounts through the wage records by where each new account's first-quarter workers came from designates Caldmere, Dunrath and Eskwell (Caldmere at 10.1), because the buyer of nineteen Caldmere stores reopened sixteen as markets with every store's staff and as many again hired, twelve Tolbeck park arrivals did the same, and eight Quarrin start-ups staffed from a closed 192-worker warehouse look like its continuation; read from the old account's side, the designation is Dunrath, Eskwell and Quarrin.
analyst_test: A strong analyst counts each county's new accounts first employing in 2026, nets off the register's predecessors and designates Caldmere, Eskwell and Tolbeck; the stronger one links the rest through the wage records by where each new account's first-quarter workers came from (more than half from one account that then stopped reporting) and designates Caldmere, Dunrath and Eskwell: the expanded take-overs read as births and the start-ups staffed from a closed payroll as continuations.
domain_test: The deciding quantity is each county's establishment birth rate as business demography defines it, a new establishment and not a continuing business under a new employer account, built from the UI account openings and quarterly wage records by the field's employment-flow continuity test read from the predecessor's side (the share of the old unit's workforce that goes on to the new identifier); with hospital or school nouns there is no employer account a business re-registers under and no workforce that moves with it, so the task stops reading the same.
layer1: several sources for one picture: the employer register, the quarterly contribution reports and the wage records
vintages: industry codes on two NAICS editions, county codes assigned from the ZIP code before the third quarter of 2025
imperfect keys: worksite addresses in two formats from the 2025 system replacement, a business's self-reported industry code on re-registration
documentation that has to be read: monthly employment on the 12th against quarterly wages, liability against registration dates, status and inactivation dates
genuine overlap: a worker on two accounts in a quarter (a job change), zero reports from open accounts, final pay after a closure

seasonal and timing texture: summer employers (a few keeping a worker through the winter), winter pauses, take-overs dated in the first days of a quarter with the old owner's final days paid in the new quarter

lineage.fate: spent 2026-10-15 at stage 4: the leak readers missed the call twice (4.5 and 8.4 per cent, the first year only) but the one re-judge after the workbook asks' FIX_NOW returned NOT_DETERMINISTIC, SEND_BACK on the graded estimates: which drugs and certificate codes make the stimulant class behind the coroner's false opioid listings was never filed, and reading the certificate's stimulant as T43.6 alone (184 against 247, 25.5 per cent) or keeping cocaine apart (189, 25.0; 21.8 or 26.7 per cent with cocaine among the other drugs) moves the 2026 count, the baseline and the change, every variant releasing phase two.
lineage.driver: A register's count of one class is wrong in both directions: it misses some of the class and files in it some units of one neighbouring class only, a class that grows while the counted one shrinks; a full review of one period measures each true class's chance of being filed in each register category, so each period's count is solved from its own register categories, the false entries scaled by the neighbouring class's own visible entries; any multiplicative correction leaves the period-on-period change untouched, and a two-way error rate pooled over every unit outside the class misplaces the false entries as the neighbouring class grows.
lineage.driver_concrete: The coroner's certificates name no drug on one overdose death in eight (an opioid death so certified is missed) and list fentanyl found but not contributing on half of the methamphetamine and cocaine deaths and on none of the other drug deaths; stimulant deaths grew from about 56 in 2021 to about 149 in 2026 while other drug deaths fell from about 83 to 61. The medical examiner's full review of 2025 gives each class's chance of each certificate category; solving each year's classes from its three certificate categories puts 2026 at 190 against a 2021 to 2023 average of 253, 24.9 per cent below, where the two-by-two correction with one false-listing rate over all non-opioid deaths files 12.1 per cent and the certificates 6.2.
